$$E_{n' n} = \left(n' + \frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar \Omega_1 + \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar \Omega_2$$
where n', n = 0, 1, 2, \ldots

Solution for subproblem(b):
 To first order in ε/k the normal-mode frequencies are
$$\Omega_1 = \omega \sqrt{1 + \frac{\varepsilon}{k}}$$
$$\Omega_2 = \omega \sqrt{1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{k}}$$
Using the first-order expansion, the energy levels are
$$E_{n' n} = \left(n' + \frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar \omega \sqrt{1 + \frac{\varepsilon}{k}} + \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar \omega \sqrt{1 - \frac{\varepsilon}{k}}$$
$$E_{n' n} \approx (n' + n + 1)\hbar \omega + (n' - n)\hbar \omega \frac{\varepsilon}{2k}$$

problem:
A particle of mass m moves with zero angular momentum (s-state, l=0) in a spherically symmetric attractive potential V(r), with radial domain 0<r<∞.

a) Write down the differential equation of radial motion for l=0, defining the radial wave function carefully and specifying the boundary conditions on it for bound states. What is the WKB eigenvalue condition for s-states in such a potential, taking into account that the motion is constrained to 0<r<∞? Use ψ(r,θ,φ)=R(r)Y_{lm}(θ,φ) with χ(r)=r R(r), and define n=0,1,2,.... Here ħ is the reduced Planck constant and h=2πħ.

b) For V(r)=-V_0 \, e^{-r/a} with V_0>0 and a>0, use the WKB relation to estimate the minimum value of V_0 such that there will be one and only one bound state, just barely bound. Compare your value to the exact result for the exponential potential, 2 m V_0 a^2 / \hbar^2 = 1.44.
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The stationary-state wave function is written as ψ(r,θ,φ)=R(r)Y_{lm}(θ,φ). For l=0 the radial equation is
$$- \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr} \left(r^2 \frac{dR}{dr}\right) + V(r) R(r) = E R(r)$$
For bound states the boundary conditions on R(r) are
$$\lim_{r \to 0} R(r) \text{ finite}$$
$$\lim_{r \to \infty} R(r) = 0$$
Defining χ(r)=r R(r) gives the one-dimensional Schrödinger equation on 0<r<∞
$$- \frac{\hbar^2}{2 m} \frac{d^2 \chi}{dr^2} + V(r) \chi = E \chi$$
with boundary conditions
$$\chi(0)=0$$
$$\lim_{r \to \infty} \chi(r) = 0$$
The WKB eigenvalue condition for s-states is
$$\oint \sqrt{2 m \left(E - V\right)} dr = \left(n + \frac{3}{4}\right) h$$
$$n=0,1,2,\dots$$

Solution for subproblem(b):
 Substituting V(r)=-V_0 e^{-r/a} into the s-wave WKB relation on 0<r<∞ gives
$$\int \sqrt{2 m \left[E + V_0 e^{- r / a}\right]} dr = \frac{1}{2} \left(n + \frac{3}{4}\right) h$$
For a bound state take
$$E = - |E|$$
The classical turning point r_t satisfies |E|=V_0 e^{-r_t/a}, so r_t=a \ln\left(V_0/|E|\right), and
$$\sqrt{2 m |E|} \int_0^{a \ln \frac{V_0}{|E|}} \sqrt{\frac{V_0}{|E|} e^{- r / a} - 1} dr = \left(n + \frac{3}{4}\right) \frac{h}{2}$$
In the limiting case of a single, just-barely-bound state we may take |E| \approx V_0, and approximate the integral by
$$\sqrt{2 m |E|} \int_0^{a \ln \frac{V_0}{|E|}} \sqrt{\frac{V_0}{|E|} e^{- r / a} - 1} dr \approx \sqrt{2 m V_0} \int_0^{a \ln \frac{V_0}{|E|}} e^{- r / (2 a)} dr$$
Evaluating the approximation gives
$$\sqrt{2 m V_0} \cdot 2 a \left(1 - \sqrt{\frac{|E|}{V_0}}\right) \approx \left(n + \frac{3}{4}\right) \frac{h}{2}$$
Using h=2πħ yields
$$\sqrt{2 m V_0} \cdot 2 a \left(1 - \sqrt{\frac{|E|}{V_0}}\right) \approx \left(n + \frac{3}{4}\right) \pi \hbar$$
Solving for E gives the WKB estimate
$$E \approx - \left[1 - \frac{\left(n + \frac{3}{4}\right) \pi \hbar}{2 a \sqrt{2 m V_0}}\right]^2 V_0$$
For one and only one bound state we require the condition to hold for n=0 but fail for n=1, i.e.
$$\frac{\frac{3}{4} \pi \hbar}{2 a \sqrt{2 m V_0}} \le 1$$
$$1 < \frac{\frac{7}{4} \pi \hbar}{2 a \sqrt{2 m V_0}}$$
The minimum V_0 satisfying these inequalities is
$$\frac{2 m V_0 a^2}{\hbar^2} = \frac{9 \pi^2}{64}$$
Numerically,
$$\frac{2 m V_0 a^2}{\hbar^2} \approx 1.39$$
which is close to the exact result for the exponential potential
$$\frac{2 m V_0 a^2}{\hbar^2} = 1.44$$

problem:
Set up the relevant equations with estimates of all missing parameters. Consider the HCl molecule as a diatomic system. Model the molecular bond as a harmonic spring with force constant K and treat the vibrational motion along a single coordinate with position operator \hat x and canonical momentum operator \hat p. Let \mu be the reduced mass of H and Cl, \omega the vibrational angular frequency, \hbar the reduced Planck constant, k the Boltzmann constant, and T the absolute temperature. Use m_p for the proton mass and approximate m_H \approx m_p and m_{Cl} \approx 35 m_p. The given parameters are $$K=470\unit{N/m}$$ $$I=2.3\times 10^{-47}\unit{kg\,m^2}$$ The rotational quantum number for a rigid rotor is J with allowed values $$J=0,1,2,\ldots$$ For part (c), if needed, define the ratio R of populations in the vibrational ground state as $$R=\frac{N_{J=0}}{N_{J=1}}$$ Use the standard constants if numerical evaluation is required $$\hbar=1.054\times 10^{-34}\unit{J\,s}$$ $$k=1.38\times 10^{-23}\unit{J/K}$$ $$m_p=1.67\times 10^{-27}\unit{kg}$$

a) At 300\unit{K} what is the probability that the molecule is in its lowest excited vibrational state?

c) Of the molecules in the vibrational ground state what is the ratio of the number in the ground rotational state to the number in the first excited rotational state?
reference_solution:
Solution for subproblem(a):
 The vibrational Hamiltonian is $$\hat H_\nu=\frac{\hat p^2}{2\mu}+\frac{1}{2}\mu\omega^2\hat x^2$$ The vibrational energy levels are $$E_\nu^{(n)}=\left(n+\frac{1}{2}\right)\hbar\omega$$ The allowed values of n are $$n=0,1,2,\ldots$$ The angular frequency is $$\omega=\sqrt{\frac{K}{\mu}}$$ In thermal equilibrium the normalized Boltzmann probability for level n can be written as $$P_n=(1-e^{-\xi})e^{-n\xi}$$ where $$\xi=\frac{\hbar\omega}{kT}$$ Hence the probability for the first excited state is $$P_1=e^{-\xi}(1-e^{-\xi})$$ The reduced mass is $$\mu=\frac{m_H m_{Cl}}{m_H+m_{Cl}}$$ Using the given approximation $$m_H\approx m_p$$ and $$m_{Cl}\approx 35 m_p$$ gives $$\mu=\frac{35}{36}m_p$$ With the numerical values $$K=470\unit{N/m}$$ $$T=300\unit{K}$$ $$m_p=1.67\times 10^{-27}\unit{kg}$$ $$\hbar=1.054\times 10^{-34}\unit{J\,s}$$ $$k=1.38\times 10^{-23}\unit{J/K}$$ we estimate $$\xi\approx 13.5$$ Therefore $$P_1\approx e^{-13.5}$$ and numerically $$P_1\approx 1.37\times 10^{-6}$$

Solution for subproblem(c):

problem:
Read the following problem and provide your answer.

a) Define M_s as the saturation magnetization density of iron/steel in SI units, meaning the magnetization at which further increase in the applied magnetic field does not increase the magnetization. Assume that, at saturation, all electron-spin magnetic moments are aligned with the applied field. Let n be the number density of spin-carrying electrons in units of \unit{m^{-3}}, and let \mu be the intrinsic-spin magnetic moment of a single electron in units of \unit{A m^2}. Use the typical values M_s = 10^6 \unit{A/m} and n = 3 \times 10^{28} \unit{m^{-3}}. Tasks: 1) State the typical saturation value for the magnetization density of iron/steel with units. 2) Using the stated assumption and given values, estimate the intrinsic-spin magnetic moment of the electron and express the final answer as \mu = ...
reference_solution:
In a ferromagnet, the magnetization increases with the applied magnetic field until it reaches the saturation magnetization M_s. At saturation, under the stated assumption, all electron-spin magnetic moments are aligned with the field, so the magnetization equals the number density of spin carriers times the single-electron moment

$$
M_s = n \mu
$$

For iron/steel, a typical saturation magnetization is

$$
M_s = 10^6 \unit{A/m}
$$

A representative electron number density is

$$
n = 3 \times 10^{28} \unit{m^{-3}}
$$

Therefore

$$
\mu = \frac{M_s}{n}
$$

Numerically

$$
\mu \approx 3 \times 10^{-23} \unit{A m^2}
$$

problem: An absorbing membrane is in thermal equilibrium, with $N$ sites available for atom adsorption, each having a potential energy of $\varepsilon_{0}$. Given the partition function of the absorbing membrane $Z_{\mathrm{s}}$, find the simplified form of the grand partition function $\Xi$ for the absorbing membrane.
reference_solution:
By substituting $Z_{\mathrm{s}}$ into the grand partition function $\Xi$, we obtain
\[
\Xi=\left[1+\exp \left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}+\varepsilon_{0}}{k T}\right)\right]^{N}
\]

Reference answer:
\[\boxed{\left[1+\exp \left(\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{s}}+\varepsilon_{0}}{k T}\right)\right]^{N}}\]

problem:
The binding energy of a nucleus has the order of magnitude  
a) \(10^{6} \mathrm{eV}\)  
b) \(10^{8} \mathrm{eV}\)  
c) \(10^{10} \mathrm{eV}\)
reference_solution:
According to the uncertainty principle \(p r \approx \frac{h}{2}\), we have \(p \approx \frac{\hbar}{2 r}\).  
The binding energy \(\approx \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}=\frac{p^{2}}{2 m}=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{8 m r^{2}} \approx \frac{6.6^{2} \times 10^{-44}}{8 \times 940\left(\frac{1.4 \times 10^{-15}}{3 \times 10^{8}}\right)^{2}}\)

\[
=2(\mathrm{MeV}) \sim 10^{6}(\mathrm{eV})
\]

Therefore, a) is the chosen answer.

Reference answer:
\boxed{a}

problem: Two magnetic dipoles $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are separated by a distance $R$. The positions of the dipoles are fixed, but their orientations can be freely chosen. They achieve thermal equilibrium with an environment at temperature $T$. In the high-temperature limit, where $\frac{M_{1} M_{2}}{k T R^{3}} \ll 1$, the system can be treated classically. The partition function is given by $Z = 16 \pi^{2} \left(1 + \frac{1}{3} \lambda^{2}\right)$. Calculate the average force $F$ between the two dipoles. Here, $\lambda = \frac{\beta M_{1} M_{2}}{R^{3}}$.

A particle with mass $m$ moves under the influence of a restoring force $-kx$ and a resistive force $-r \dot{x}$ (where both $k$ and $r$ are positive constants), where $x$ is the displacement of the particle from its equilibrium position. If $r < r_{0}$, is it possible for the particle to return to the equilibrium position more quickly for certain initial conditions compared to when $r = r_{0}$?
reference_solution:
When $r < r_{0}$, it is the underdamped case, and the general solution is

$$
x(t) = A e^{-\frac{r}{2m} t} \cos \left(\omega_{d} t + \alpha\right)
$$

where

$$
\omega_{d} = \sqrt{k/m - \left(\frac{r}{2m}\right)^{2}}
$$

Since $r < r_{0}$, it is impossible for the particle to return to the equilibrium position more quickly under any initial conditions than in the critically damped case.

Reference answer:
\boxed{No}

problem:
In a vacuum chamber, a collimated beam of $\mathrm{Na}^{23}$ atoms (obtained by evaporating a solid sample at $10^{3} \mathrm{~K}$) is irradiated by a high-intensity laser beam. The laser frequency is chosen such that sodium atoms with velocity $v_{0}$ can resonantly absorb photons from the laser.

After the emission of a photon, the atom will deflect relative to its pre-emission motion direction.

(3) What is the maximum deflection angle $\varphi_{\text{max}}$ of the atom relative to its pre-emission motion direction, after a single photon emission?

A gyroscope has a central inertia ellipsoid with a rotational symmetry axis, and the moments of inertia are given by \(I_{1} = I_{2} = 2I_{3}\). It is undergoing free motion about a fixed point around its center of mass, with an intrinsic angular velocity \(\omega_{1}\). The angle between the spin axis and the precession axis is \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\). Please use Euler's equations of motion to determine the precession angular velocity \(\omega_{2}\).

Consider a non-interacting non-relativistic electron gas. Determine the density of states $N(E)$ (where $E$ is the energy) when the particles are constrained to move within a planar region of area $A$.
reference_solution:
Consider a square region with side length $L$ (where $L^{2}=A$). The eigenfunctions of the particles are

$$
\sin \frac{n_{x} \pi x}{L} \sin \frac{n_{y} \pi y}{L},\left\{\begin{array}{l}
n_{x}=1,2, \cdots \\
n_{y}=1,2, \cdots
\end{array}\right.
$$

The energy levels are

$$
E\left(n_{x}, n_{y}\right)=\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 m} \cdot \frac{\pi^{2}}{L^{2}}\left(n_{x}^{2}+n_{y}^{2}\right) \equiv \frac{\hbar^{2}}{2 m} \frac{\pi^{2}}{L^{2}} n^{2} \equiv E(n)
$$

The number of states between $n$ and $n+\mathrm{d} n$ is

$$
2 \cdot \frac{1}{4} \cdot 2 \pi n \mathrm{~d} n=\pi n \mathrm{~d} n
$$

Therefore, the density of states is

$$
N(E) = \pi n \frac{\mathrm{d} n}{\mathrm{d} E} = \frac{A}{2 \pi} \left( \frac{2 m}{\hbar^2} \right) E^{-1/2}
$$

Reference answer:
\[\boxed{\frac{A}{2 \pi} \left( \frac{2 m}{\hbar^2} \right) E^{-1/2}}\]

problem: A long thin wire carries a current $I$ and is located at a distance $d$ from a semi-infinite iron block. Assume the permeability of the iron block is infinite. Suppose the magnitude of the image current inside the iron block is $I^{\prime}$, located at $x=-d$. Determine the magnitude and direction of $I^{\prime}$.
reference_solution:
We solve this using the method of images. Let the image current be $I^{\prime}$, located at $x=-d$, with its direction opposite to that of $I$. Its magnitude is given by

$$
I^{\prime}=\frac{\mu-\mu_{0}}{\mu+\mu_{0}} I.
$$

Since $\mu \rightarrow \infty$, it follows that $I^{\prime}=I$.

Reference answer:
\boxed{I}

problem: A space station with mass $m$ orbits the moon along a circular orbit with radius $R$. To enable the space station to land on the moon, an object with mass $m_{1}$ is launched in the forward direction along the orbital curve, so that after the space station has turned through an angle of $180^{\circ}$, it reaches the surface of the moon. Given the mass of the moon $M_{\mathrm{m}}$ and its radius $R_{\mathrm{m}}$, determine the launch velocity of the object with mass $m_{1}$.

The average lifetime of a stationary muon is $2.197 \times 10^{-6} \mathrm{~s}$. In cosmic rays, the speed of muons can reach $0.99 c$ (where $c$ is the speed of light in a vacuum). Calculate the average distance that such high-speed muons can travel as observed from an observer on Earth using the time dilation effect.
reference_solution:
Method Two: Using the time dilation effect. In the $S^{\prime}$ frame, muon decay occurs at the same location, and the clock in the $S^{\prime}$ frame is the moving clock,

$$
\tau_{0} = \tau \sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}, \quad \tau = \frac{\tau_{0}}{\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{v}{c}\right)^{2}}}
$$

The following is the same as Method One.

Reference answer:
\boxed{435.7}

problem:
Derive in detail all the calculations of Hardy's theorem. Consider a two-spin $1/2$ system, and express an arbitrary entangled state $|\Psi\rangle \in H_{AB}$ in the orthonormal basis $\left\{|u\rangle_{1},|v\rangle_{1}\right\}$ for particle 1:

$$
|\Psi\rangle = |u\rangle_{1}\left|\phi_{u}\right\rangle_{2} + |v\rangle_{1}\left|\phi_{v}\right\rangle_{2}
$$

where $\left|\phi_{u}\right\rangle_{2} \neq 0$, and $\left|\phi_{v}\right\rangle_{2}$ is neither orthogonal nor parallel to $\left|\phi_{u}\right\rangle_{2}$, i.e.,

$$
|\phi\rangle_{2} = \alpha\left|\phi_{u}\right\rangle_{2} + \left|\phi_{u}^{\perp}\right\rangle_{2}, \quad \alpha \neq 0
$$

with $\left|\phi_{u}^{\perp}\right\rangle_{2} \neq 0$ and $\left\langle\phi_{u} \mid \phi_{u}^{\perp}\right\rangle = 0$. Hence, a suitable basis $|u\rangle_{i}, |v\rangle_{i}, i=1,2$ can be chosen so that $|\Psi\rangle$ is written in the form:

$$
|\Psi\rangle = a|v\rangle_{1}|v\rangle_{2} + b|u\rangle_{1}|v\rangle_{2} + c|v\rangle_{1}|u\rangle_{2}, \quad abc \neq 0
$$

Define the observables:

$$
U_{i} \equiv |u\rangle_{ii}\langle u|, \quad W_{i} \equiv |\beta\rangle_{ii}\langle\beta|, \quad i=1,2
$$

where

$$
|\beta\rangle_{1} = \frac{a|v\rangle_{1} + b|u\rangle_{1}}{\sqrt{|a|^{2} + |b|^{2}}}
$$

It can be easily verified that the following measurement result holds: (2) $U_{1} = 0 \Rightarrow W_{2} = 1$.
Consider the operator $\hat{F}$ with the integral kernel $F(x, x^{\prime}) = f(x) f^{*}(x^{\prime})$. Find the eigenvalues and eigenstates of this operator.
Use action variables and angle variables to find the frequencies of a three-dimensional harmonic oscillator with different force constants.
reference_solution:
$$
\nu_{1}=\frac{\partial H^{*}}{\partial J_{1}}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{m}}, \\
\nu_{2}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{k_{2}}{m}}, \quad \nu_{3}=\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{k_{3}}{m}}.
$$

Reference answer:
\boxed{\frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{m}}, \frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{k_{2}}{m}}, \frac{1}{2 \pi} \sqrt{\frac{k_{3}}{m}}}

problem: In interstellar space, there is a cloud of hydrogen atoms with a density of $\rho$ and a temperature of $T$. Find the natural width of the light resulting from the transition from the ground state to the 2p state.
For the various s states of a hydrogen atom $(n, l, m) = (n, 0, 0)$, calculate $\Delta x$ and discuss the case when $n \gg 1$.
reference_solution:
Due to the isotropy of the s state, we have:

$$
\langle x \rangle = 0, \quad \left\langle x^{2} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{3} \left\langle r^{2} \right\rangle
$$

The average value of $r^{2}$ can be calculated using the Kramers relation; for the s state, it is:

$$
\left\langle r^{2} \right\rangle_{n00} = \frac{n^{2}}{2} \left(1+5 n^{2}\right) a_{0}^{2}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\Delta x = \sqrt{\left\langle x^{2} \right\rangle} = \frac{\sqrt{\left\langle r^{2} \right\rangle}}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{n}{\sqrt{6}} \sqrt{1+5 n^{2}} a_{0}
$$

When $n \gg 1$

$$
\Delta x = \sqrt{\frac{5}{6}} n a_{0}
$$

Reference answer:
\boxed{\frac{n}{\sqrt{6}} \sqrt{1+5 n^{2}}, \sqrt{\frac{5}{6}} n}

problem: In the eigenstate of $S_{z}$ being +1, when measuring spin along the direction of $\boldsymbol{n}(\theta, \varphi)$, what are the possible values that can be obtained?
reference_solution:
Express $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}$ using the Pauli matrices, obtaining the following representation:

$$
\sigma_{n}=\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}=\left(\begin{array}{cc}
\cos \theta & \sin \theta \mathrm{e}^{-i \varphi} \\
\sin \theta \mathrm{e}^{i \varphi} & -\cos \theta
\end{array}\right), \quad \boldsymbol{n}=(\sin \theta \cos \varphi, \sin \theta \sin \varphi, \cos \theta)
$$

Its eigenvalues are $\pm 1$, with corresponding eigenvectors:

$$
\chi_{+}=\binom{\cos \frac{\theta}{2}}{\sin \frac{\theta}{2} \mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{i} \varphi}}, \quad \chi_{-}=\binom{-\sin \frac{\theta}{2} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i} \varphi}}{\cos \frac{\theta}{2}}
$$

The electron is in the state $\chi_{1 / 2}\left(S_{z}=1\right)=\binom{1}{0}$, so the possible measurement values of $\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \boldsymbol{n}$ are $\pm 1$.

Reference answer:
\boxed{1, -1}

problem:
Derive the effective scattering cross section of the radiation using the radiation pressure \( P \) of this wave.

\[
\sigma = \frac{\langle F\rangle}{P}
\]

For a plane electromagnetic wave, \( P = \frac{|S|}{c}, \langle P \rangle = \frac{\langle S \rangle}{c} \).
reference_solution:
Thus, the effective scattering cross section is obtained as

\[
\sigma = \frac{\langle F\rangle}{\langle P\rangle} = \frac{e^{4}}{12 \pi^{2} c^{4} \varepsilon_{0}^{2} m^{2}} = \frac{4}{3} r_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}
\]

where \( r_{c} \) is the classical radius of the electron.

Reference answer:
\boxed{\frac{4}{3} r_{\mathrm{c}}^{2}}

problem:
Which of the following options accurately describes the nature of an unpolarized beam of electrons?
(A) It can be described by a wave function composed of two equal parts of spin-up and spin-down components.
(B) It cannot be described by a wave function.
(C) It can be described using classical mechanics.

The vertical acceleration of a certain solid-fuel rocket is given by

$$
a = k \mathrm{e}^{-b t} - c v - g
$$

where $b, c, k$ are constants, $v$ is the acquired vertical velocity, and $g$ is the gravitational acceleration. When operating in the atmosphere, $g$ is considered a constant. Use the method of integrating factors to determine the vertical velocity $v$ of the rocket after $t$ seconds from launch.

For the reaction $\mathrm{p}+\mathrm{p} \rightarrow \pi^{+}+\mathrm{D}$, the differential cross-section at a center-of-mass energy $E$ is given by $\frac{\mathrm{d} \sigma}{\mathrm{d} \Omega} = A + B \cos^2 \theta$. Determine the differential cross-section for the inverse reaction $\pi^{+} + \mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{p} + \mathrm{p}$ at the same energy. (This has been measured experimentally for unpolarized beams.)
reference_solution:
For a reaction $\mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D}$ and its inverse reaction $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{D} \rightarrow \mathrm{A} + \mathrm{B}$, disregarding constant factors, we have

$|M_{if}|$, the transition matrix element. The transition matrix elements for the direct and inverse reactions should be invariant under the action of the time reversal operator. That is, the time reversal operator only reverses the spin and changes the direction of the momentum. Thus, the amplitude of the reaction process 

$$
\left(\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{A}, \boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{B}, \boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{A}, \boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{B}\right) \rightarrow \left(\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{C}, \boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{D}, \boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{C}, \boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{D}\right)
$$

equals the amplitude after time reversal

$$
\left(-\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{C}, -\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{D}, -\boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{C}, -\boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{D}\right) \rightarrow \left(-\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{A}, -\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{B}, -\boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{A}, -\boldsymbol{s}_\mathrm{B}\right)
$$

In cross-section measurements, the spin is not measured. Assuming the initial state beam is unpolarized, one sums over all spins for the final state and averages over all initial state spins. However, here we sum over all spins, giving

Since the ratio of cross-sections for the direct and inverse reactions is independent of the details of the reaction, for the direct reaction, the incident beam flow is $\left(\frac{p_\mathrm{A}}{E_\mathrm{A}} + \frac{p_\mathrm{B}}{E_\mathrm{B}}\right)$, and for the inverse reaction, it is $\left(\frac{p_\mathrm{C}}{E_\mathrm{C}} + \frac{p_\mathrm{D}}{E_\mathrm{D}}\right)$. The phase space factor for the final state of the direct reaction is proportional to 

$$
p_f^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}p_f}{\mathrm{d}E} = \frac{\left(p_{f_1}\right)^2}{\left(\frac{p_\mathrm{C}}{E_\mathrm{C}}\right) + \left(\frac{p_\mathrm{D}}{E_\mathrm{D}}\right)} \quad p_{f_1} = |\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{C}| = |\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{D}|
$$

Similarly, we obtain the phase space factor for the inverse reaction

$$
p_f^2 \frac{\mathrm{d}p_f}{\mathrm{d}E} = \frac{\left(p_{f_2}\right)^2}{\left(\frac{p_\mathrm{A}}{E_\mathrm{A}}\right) + \left(\frac{p_\mathrm{B}}{E_\mathrm{B}}\right)} \quad p_{f_2} = |\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{A}| = |\boldsymbol{p}_\mathrm{B}|
$$

Since we average over all initial state spins, each reaction's final state spin degrees of freedom should be included, resulting in the final outcome

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{(\mathrm{d} \sigma / \mathrm{d} \Omega)_{\text{forward}}}{(\mathrm{d} \sigma / \mathrm{d} \Omega)_{\text{reverse}}} & = \frac{\left(p_{f_1}\right)^2 (2s_\mathrm{C} + 1)(2s_\mathrm{D} + 1)}{\left(p_{f_2}\right)^2 (2s_\mathrm{A} + 1)(2s_\mathrm{B} + 1)} = \frac{3 p_\mathrm{C}^2}{4 p_\mathrm{A}^2} \\
& = \frac{3}{4} \left\{\frac{\left(E^2 - m_{\pi}^2 - m_\mathrm{D}^2\right)^2 - 4 m_{\pi}^2 m_\mathrm{D}^2}{E^2 \left(E^2 - 4 m_\mathrm{D}^2\right)}\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Reference answer:
\boxed{\frac{3}{4} \left\{\frac{\left(E^2 - m_{\pi}^2 - m_\mathrm{D}^2\right)^2 - 4 m_{\pi}^2 m_\mathrm{D}^2}{E^2 \left(E^2 - 4 m_\mathrm{D}^2\right)}\right\}}

problem: Consider a one-dimensional vibrating lattice at absolute zero, with an atomic number density of \(n\) and mass \(m\). Using the Debye approximation and assuming all acoustic modes have the same speed \(v\), calculate the average strain \(\overline{\left(\frac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right)^{2}}\).
reference_solution:
\[
\left(\frac{\partial r_{j}}{\partial x}\right)^{2}=q_{j}^{2} r_{0 j}^{2} \sin ^{2}\left(q_{j} x-\omega_{j} t\right)
\]

For the \(j\)th atom, the time-averaged square is:

\[
\overline{\left(\frac{\partial r_{j}}{\partial x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{1}{2} q_{j}^{2} r_{0 j}^{2}
\]

According to the average kinetic energy of atomic vibration, which equals half of its total energy:

\[
r_{0 j}^{2}=\frac{\hbar}{2 m \omega_{j}}
\]

Substituting into the above equation:

\[
\overline{\left(\frac{\partial r_{j}}{\partial x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{\hbar \omega_{j}}{4 m v^{2}}
\]

Averaging over all atoms in the one-dimensional lattice:

\[
\overline{\left(\frac{\partial R}{\partial x}\right)^{2}}=\frac{\hbar \omega_{\mathrm{D}}^{2}}{8 n m v^{3}}
\]

Reference answer:
\boxed{\frac{\hbar \omega_{\mathrm{D}}^{2}}{8 n m v^{3}}}

\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Interpret the requested ordering literally}

The eleven expressions in the question are candidate terms, not a complete
basis for the eight-dimensional anomaly. In particular, with curvature
weights

\[
[P]=2,\qquad [B]=4,\qquad [O]=[\Omega]=6,
\]

only scalars of total weight eight can contribute to $X^{(4)}$. This
immediately rules out
$\operatorname{tr}(P^3)$, $\operatorname{tr}(BP)$,
$\operatorname{tr}(B^2P)$, $\operatorname{tr}(OP^2)$, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Omega)$. It is important not to replace the published
ordering by a different set of invariants: the requested output is the
coefficient of each listed candidate in exactly the order printed in the
problem.

\subparagraph*{1. Convert the Schouten normalization}

The conventional Schouten tensor is

\[
S_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{d-2}
\left(R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{R}{2(d-1)}\gamma_{\mu\nu}\right).
\]

Thus the tensor denoted by $P$ in the question is $P=(d-2)S$, and at
$d=8$,

\[
S=\frac{P}{6},\qquad J\equiv\operatorname{tr}S
=\frac{\operatorname{tr}P}{6}.
\]

The question's $B$ is the conventionally normalized Bach tensor. For the
extended obstruction tensors,

\[
\Omega^{(1)}=-\frac14 B,
\qquad
\Omega^{(2)}=\frac18 O
\qquad (d=8).
\]

These relations follow from the standard formulas for extended obstruction
tensors in
\href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/abs/0810.4203}}{Graham}.

\subparagraph*{2. Use the eight-dimensional anomaly density}

In conventional Schouten normalization, the Einstein-gravity result is

\[
\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle
\begin{aligned}
X^{(4)}={}&
 \frac18\operatorname{tr}(S^4)
-\frac16J\operatorname{tr}(S^3)
-\frac1{16}\big[\operatorname{tr}(S^2)\big]^2
+\frac18J^2\operatorname{tr}(S^2)
-\frac1{48}J^4 \\
&+\frac16J\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Omega^{(1)}S\right)
-\frac16\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Omega^{(1)}S^2\right)
+\frac1{24}\operatorname{tr}\!\left[(\Omega^{(1)})^2\right]
+\frac1{24}\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Omega^{(2)}S\right).
\end{aligned}$}
\]

This is the $8d$ holographic Weyl-anomaly formula of
\href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.14014}}{Jia and Karydas}, with
$\kappa^2=8\pi G$. Substituting $S=P/6$,
$\Omega^{(1)}=-B/4$, and $\Omega^{(2)}=O/8$ gives

\[
\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle
\begin{aligned}
X^{(4)}={}&
 \frac1{10368}\operatorname{tr}(P^4)
-\frac1{20736}\big[\operatorname{tr}(P^2)\big]^2
-\frac1{7776}\operatorname{tr}(P^3)\operatorname{tr}(P)\\
&+\frac1{10368}\operatorname{tr}(P^2)
  \big[\operatorname{tr}(P)\big]^2
-\frac1{62208}\big[\operatorname{tr}(P)\big]^4\\
&-\frac1{864}\operatorname{tr}(BP)\operatorname{tr}(P)
+\frac1{864}\operatorname{tr}(BP^2)
+\frac1{384}\operatorname{tr}(B^2)
+\frac1{1152}\operatorname{tr}(OP).
\end{aligned}$}
\]

This full expression also shows why the candidate list is not a complete
basis: several nonzero pure-$P$ invariants and
$\operatorname{tr}(BP)\operatorname{tr}(P)$ are not among the eleven items
printed in the question.

\subparagraph*{3. Read off the requested coefficients}

For the exact ordering

\[
\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle
\begin{gathered}
\operatorname{tr}(P^4),\ \operatorname{tr}(P^3),\
\operatorname{tr}(P^3)\operatorname{tr}(P),\ \operatorname{tr}(BP),\
\operatorname{tr}(BP^2),\ \operatorname{tr}(B^2),\\
\operatorname{tr}(B^2P),\ \operatorname{tr}(OP),\
\operatorname{tr}(OP^2),\ \operatorname{tr}(\Omega),\
\operatorname{tr}(\Omega P),
\end{gathered}$}
\].

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{
\left[
\frac{1}{10368},\ 0,\ -\frac{1}{7776},\ 0,\
\frac{1}{864},\ \frac{1}{384},\ 0,\ \frac{1}{1152},\ 0,\ 0,\ 0
\right]
}
\]

\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

We use the standard cell-autonomous interpretation: along a lineage, the semi-Markov growth-rate process continues independently of division, while descendant branches subsequently evolve independently. Division noise is independent of the growth-rate process. Gamma-driven telegraph processes are naturally treated as alternating renewal processes; their moment-generating functions can be obtained using renewal equations \href{\detokenize{https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/EBD1A21E96B138EDF54FDE0275B7B069/S0001867821000549a.pdf/some_results_on_the_telegraph_process_driven_by_gamma_components.pdf}}{Martinucci, Meoli, and Zacks}. Size regulation correlates successive generation times, so a naive uncorrelated Euler-Lotka equation is not appropriate \href{\detokenize{https://journals.aps.org/pre/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevE.103.L060402}}{Pigolotti, 2021}.

\subparagraph*{1. Size dynamics and homeostasis}

After symmetric division, the next birth size is

\[
v_{b,n+1}=\frac{v_{d,n}}{2} =v_{b,n}^{1-\beta}\bar v_b^\beta+\frac{\xi_n}{2}.
\]

Define

\[
x_n=\frac{v_{b,n}}{\bar v_b}, \qquad \epsilon_n=\frac{\xi_n}{2\bar v_b}.
\]

Then

\[
x_{n+1}=x_n^{1-\beta}+\epsilon_n,
\]

with

\[
\left\langle\epsilon_n\right\rangle=0, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon_n)=\frac{\sigma^2}{4\bar v_b^2}.
\]

For small fluctuations, write $x_n=1+\delta_n$. To leading order,

\[
\delta_{n+1}=(1-\beta)\delta_n+\epsilon_n+O(\delta_n^2).
\]

Because $0<\beta\leq1$,

\[
|1-\beta|<1,
\]

so the birth-size distribution is stationary. Its leading variance is

\[
\operatorname{Var}(\delta) = \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)} {1-(1-\beta)^2} = \frac{\sigma^2} {4\bar v_b^2\beta(2-\beta)} +O\!\left(\frac{\sigma^4}{\bar v_b^4}\right).
\]

Thus the narrow-noise expansion requires more precisely

\[
\frac{\sigma^2} {4\bar v_b^2\beta(2-\beta)}\ll1.
\]

\subparagraph*{2. Why division-size noise does not change the exponent}

Let

\[
A(t)=\int_0^t\lambda_s\,ds
\]

be the accumulated logarithmic single-cell growth, and let $D(t)$ be the number of divisions along a forward lineage.

Since every division halves the size of the selected daughter,

\[
v(t)=v(0)\frac{e^{A(t)}}{2^{D(t)}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
2^{D(t)} = e^{A(t)}\frac{v(0)}{v(t)}.
\]

For symmetric binary division, the many-to-one identity gives

\[
\mathbb E[N(t)] = \mathbb E_{\mathrm{lin}}\!\left[2^{D(t)}\right].
\]

Consequently,

\[
\mathbb E[N(t)] = v(0)\, \mathbb E_{\mathrm{lin}} \left[ \frac{e^{A(t)}}{v(t)} \right].
\]

Because $\beta>0$ produces a stationary, time-independent cell-size distribution, $v(0)/v(t)$ contributes only a subexponential factor. Hence

\[
\Lambda = \lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{1}{t} \ln\mathbb E\!\left[ e^{\int_0^t\lambda_s\,ds} \right].
\]

Thus $\Lambda$ is the scaled cumulant-generating function of the integrated growth rate at conjugate parameter $q=1$. The size-control rule, $\beta$, $\bar v_b$, and $\sigma^2$ do not enter this exponent. This biomass-population-growth connection for symmetric, size-homeostatic division is also consistent with established cell-size-control results \href{\detokenize{https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cels.2017.08.015}}{Lin and Amir, 2017}.

\subparagraph*{3. Renewal equation for the two-state growth process}

Let $M_\pm(t)$ be

\[
M_\pm(t) = \mathbb E_\pm \left[ e^{\int_0^t\lambda_s\,ds} \right],
\]

when the process begins at the start of a $\pm$ sojourn. Let

\[
\overline F_\pm(t)=1-\int_0^t f_\pm(u)\,du
\]

be the corresponding survival probability.

Conditioning on the first switching time gives

\[
M_+(t) = e^{\lambda^+t}\overline F_+(t) + \int_0^t f_+(u)e^{\lambda^+u}M_-(t-u)\,du,
\]

and similarly,

\[
M_-(t) = e^{\lambda^-t}\overline F_-(t) + \int_0^t f_-(u)e^{\lambda^-u}M_+(t-u)\,du.
\]

Taking a Laplace transform in $t$, the common denominator is

\[
1- \widehat f_+(s-\lambda^+) \widehat f_-(s-\lambda^-).
\]

The dominant real singularity $s=\Lambda$ therefore satisfies

\[
\widehat f_+(\Lambda-\lambda^+) \widehat f_-(\Lambda-\lambda^-)=1.
\]

For the gamma waiting-time density,

\[
\widehat f_\pm(z) = \int_0^\infty e^{-zt}f_\pm(t)\,dt = \left(\frac{k_\pm}{k_\pm+z}\right)^\alpha.
\]

Hence

\[
\left[ \frac{k_+k_-} {\left(k_++\Lambda-\lambda^+\right) \left(k_-+\Lambda-\lambda^-\right)} \right]^\alpha =1.
\]

At the dominant real root all factors are positive. Since $\alpha>0$,

\[
\left(k_++\Lambda-\lambda^+\right) \left(k_-+\Lambda-\lambda^-\right) =k_+k_-.
\]

Expanding gives the quadratic equation

\[
\Lambda^2 + \left(k_++k_- -\lambda^+-\lambda^-\right)\Lambda + (k_+-\lambda^+)(k_--\lambda^-)-k_+k_- =0.
\]

The asymptotic growth rate is the larger root:

\[
\Lambda_0 = \frac{1}{2} \left[ \lambda^++\lambda^--k_+-k_- + \sqrt{ \left(\lambda^+-\lambda^- -k_+ +k_-\right)^2 +4k_+k_- } \right].
\]

The common gamma shape $\alpha$ cancels. It affects transient and correlation properties, but not this dominant exponent. If the two states had different shape parameters, such a cancellation would not generally occur.

\subparagraph*{4. Small division-noise expansion}

Since the division rule enters only through a stationary size factor,

\[
\Lambda = \Lambda_0 + 0\cdot\frac{\sigma^2}{\bar v_b^2} + O\!\left(\frac{\sigma^4}{\bar v_b^4}\right).
\]

In fact, within the stated symmetric, size-homeostatic model, the independence is exact to all algebraic orders. The neglected Gaussian events producing unphysical division sizes are exponentially rare in $\bar v_b^2/\sigma^2$ and are outside the perturbative expansion.

Increasing $\sigma^2$ broadens the cell-size distribution, while increasing $\beta$ strengthens size regulation and reduces that broadening:

\[
\frac{\operatorname{Var}(v_b)}{\bar v_b^2} \simeq \frac{\sigma^2} {4\bar v_b^2\beta(2-\beta)}.
\]

Neither changes the asymptotic population growth rate to first order.

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
\Lambda=\frac{\lambda_++\lambda_- -k_+-k_-+
\sqrt{(\lambda_+-\lambda_- -k_+ +k_-)^2+4k_+k_-}}{2},\\
(\mathrm{answer}_{\beta},\mathrm{answer}_{\sigma^2})=(\mathrm{C},\mathrm{C})
\end{gathered}
}
\]

\begin{equation}

\end{equation}
with $\phi \sim \phi + 2\pi$ and $\tau_E \sim \tau_E + \beta = \tau_E + \frac{2\pi}{r_0}$, and this geometry is terminated by a spherically symmetric brane of tension $\eta$, where $0<\eta<1$, behind the horizon. Let $\mathcal{O}(x)$ be a scalar primary operator in the BCFT, whose bulk dual is a massive scalar field of mass $m$. # Main problem:

\subsubsection*{Solution}
The geodesic prescription for a heavy scalar operator is

\[
\langle \mathcal O(x)\rangle \simeq \mathcal A_{\mathcal O}\,e^{-mL_{\mathrm{ren}}},
\]

where $L_{\mathrm{ren}}$ is the renormalized proper length of the geodesic joining the asymptotic boundary to the end-of-the-world brane. The factor $\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}$ denotes a normalization and possible subleading WKB prefactor; the geodesic approximation fixes the leading exponential dependence but does not by itself prove that this prefactor is independent of $m$, $r_0$, or $\eta$. The answer template uses the conventional leading-order normalization $\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}=1$. This is the WKB prescription used for one-point functions in these single-sided BTZ geometries \href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.12219}}{Geng-Jiang, Eqs. (2.11)-(2.12)}.

\subparagraph*{1. Brane turning point}

For an ETW brane obeying the constant-tension condition

\[
Kh_{ab}-K_{ab}=\eta h_{ab},
\]

spherical symmetry means that the brane wraps the $\phi$ circle and has a trajectory $(r(\ell),\tau_E(\ell))$, where $\ell$ is proper length. Its normalization condition is

\[
f(r)\dot{\tau}_E^{\,2}+\frac{\dot r^{\,2}}{f(r)}=1.
\]

The brane equation reduces to

\[
\dot r^{\,2}=f(r)-\eta^2r^2 =(1-\eta^2)r^2-r_0^2.
\]

At the time-reflection-symmetric turning point, $\dot r=0$. Therefore,

\[
(1-\eta^2)r_c^2-r_0^2=0,
\]

so that

\[
r_c=\frac{r_0}{\sqrt{1-\eta^2}}.
\]

This agrees with the explicit constant-tension brane solution derived in \href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.12219}}{Appendix A of Geng-Jiang}. Notice that $r_c\ge r_0$, with $r_c\to\infty$ as $\eta\to1^{-}$.

\subparagraph*{2. Geodesic length}

At $\tau_E=0$, spherical symmetry forces the dominant zero-angular-momentum geodesic to lie at fixed $\phi$. On the spatial slice,

\[
ds=\frac{dr}{\sqrt{r^2-r_0^2}}.
\]

Because the brane replaces the second exterior, the geodesic runs from the boundary cutoff $r_\epsilon$ to the Euclidean horizon $r_0$, and then from $r_0$ to the brane turning point $r_c$. Hence

\[
L_\epsilon = \int_{r_0}^{r_\epsilon}\frac{dr}{\sqrt{r^2-r_0^2}} + \int_{r_0}^{r_c}\frac{dr}{\sqrt{r^2-r_0^2}}.
\]

Using

\[
\int_{r_0}^{R}\frac{dr}{\sqrt{r^2-r_0^2}} = \operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{R}{r_0}\right),
\]

we obtain

\[
L_\epsilon = \operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{r_\epsilon}{r_0}\right) + \operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{r_c}{r_0}\right).
\]

For $r_\epsilon\to\infty$,

\[
\operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{r_\epsilon}{r_0}\right) = \log\left(\frac{2r_\epsilon}{r_0}\right)+O(r_\epsilon^{-2}).
\]

Furthermore,

\[
\operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{r_c}{r_0}\right) = \operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\eta^2}}\right).
\]

Since

\[
\cosh(\operatorname{arctanh}\eta) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\eta^2}},
\]

this becomes

\[
\operatorname{arcosh}\left(\frac{r_c}{r_0}\right) = \operatorname{arctanh}\eta = \frac12\log\left(\frac{1+\eta}{1-\eta}\right).
\]

Subtracting the universal boundary divergence $\log r_\epsilon$ gives

\[
L_{\mathrm{ren}} = \log\left(\frac{2}{r_0}\right) + \operatorname{arctanh}\eta.
\]

\subparagraph*{3. One-point function}

Consequently,

\[
\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle \begin{aligned}
\langle\mathcal O(x)\rangle
&\simeq
\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}
\exp\left[
-m\left(
\log\frac{2}{r_0}
+\operatorname{arctanh}\eta
\right)
\right] \\[2mm]
&=
\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}
\left(\frac{r_0}{2}\right)^m
e^{-m\operatorname{arctanh}\eta} \\[2mm]
&=
\mathcal A_{\mathcal O}
\left(\frac{r_0}{2}\right)^m
\left(\frac{1-\eta}{1+\eta}\right)^{m/2}.
\end{aligned}$}
\]

Since $r_0=2\pi/\beta$, this can equivalently be written as

\[
\langle\mathcal O(x)\rangle \simeq \mathcal A_{\mathcal O} \left(\frac{\pi}{\beta}\right)^m \left(\frac{1-\eta}{1+\eta}\right)^{m/2}.
\]

The leading result is independent of the spatial position $x=\phi$ because both the BTZ geometry and the brane are rotationally invariant. Its dependence on $m$ is exponential through $e^{-mL_{\mathrm{ren}}}$. At fixed normalization and renormalization scheme, increasing $\eta$ lengthens the geodesic and suppresses the one-point function. In particular,

\[
\eta=0: \qquad \langle\mathcal O\rangle \simeq \mathcal A_{\mathcal O}\left(\frac{r_0}{2}\right)^m,
\]

whereas $\langle\mathcal O\rangle\to0$ as $\eta\to1^-$.

For a scalar in AdS$_3$ of unit radius, its conformal dimension obeys

\[
m^2=\Delta(\Delta-2), \qquad \Delta=1+\sqrt{1+m^2}.
\]

At leading WKB order, $\Delta\simeq m$; if one uses $\Delta$ as the geodesic exponent convention, one replaces $m$ by $\Delta$ in the formula above.

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{
\left\langle\mathcal O(x)\right\rangle
=\left(\frac{r_0}{2}\right)^m
\left(\frac{1-\eta}{1+\eta}\right)^{m/2}
}
\]

# Problem setup:
High-harmonic generation (HHG) is a nonlinear optical process in which intense laser fields interact with gas-phase atoms or molecules to produce coherent extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation. In this setup, a sequence of time-delayed laser pulses are focused into a gas jet to investigate the role of structured light in controlling the HHG process.

# Main problem:

I create a driving field composed of three temporally identical laser pulses of 800 nm center wavelength, 50 fs FWHM pulse duration, with the peaks of the pulses at t = 0 fs, t = 30 fs, and t = 60 fs, respectively. The first pulse is left circularly polarized and carries an orbital angular momentum (OAM) of  $\ell = -1$, the second pulse is right circularly polarized and has OAM $\ell = 2$, and the third pulse is left circularly polarized and has OAM $\ell = 1$. The pulses are focused, overlapped in space, into a gas jet, and used to drive high-harmonic generation to produce EUV light. Calculate the OAM of the 23rd harmonic order and give the associated helicity $\sigma$ ($\pm 1$).
reference_solution:
\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

\subparagraph*{1. Represent the driving field}

Let $\sigma=+1$ denote left-circular polarization and $\sigma=-1$ right-circular polarization. The three pulses therefore have

\[
(\ell_1,\sigma_1)=(-1,+1),\qquad (\ell_2,\sigma_2)=(2,-1),\qquad (\ell_3,\sigma_3)=(1,+1).
\]

Their positive-frequency field is schematically

\[
\mathbf E^{(+)}(\rho,\phi,t) = \sum_{j=1}^{3} E_j(\rho)f(t-t_j) e^{i\ell_j\phi} \mathbf e_{\sigma_j} e^{-i\omega_0t+i\varphi_j},
\]

where $t_j=(0,30,60)\,\mathrm{fs}$ and $\varphi_j$ are the relative carrier phases.

Because this sum contains different $\ell_j$ and $\sigma_j$, it is not an eigenstate of either OAM or helicity during temporal overlap.

\subparagraph*{2. The pulses overlap significantly}

Assuming the quoted $50\,\mathrm{fs}$ duration is the intensity FWHM of a Gaussian pulse,

\[
\frac{I_j(t)}{I_0} = \exp\left[ -4\ln 2\left(\frac{t-t_j}{50\,\mathrm{fs}}\right)^2 \right].
\]

At a separation of $30\,\mathrm{fs}$,

\[
\frac{I(t_j\pm30\,\mathrm{fs})}{I_0} = \exp\left[-4\ln2\left(\frac{30}{50}\right)^2\right] = 0.368567304323.
\]

Thus adjacent pulses retain about $36.9\%$ of their peak intensity at one another's peak. They cannot generally be treated as independent. Time-delayed vortex drivers are known to produce harmonics with time-dependent or distributed OAM rather than one fixed topological charge; this is the basis of HHG self-torque (\href{\detokenize{https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acsphotonics.4c01320}}{ACS Photonics}).

\subparagraph*{3. Allowed photon channels for harmonic 23}

Let $n_j$ be the number of fundamental photons drawn from pulse $j$ in a particular lowest-order photon channel. Since all pulses have the same frequency $\omega_0$,

\[
n_1+n_2+n_3=23.
\]

For an isotropic gas returning to the same internal state, spin and orbital angular momenta of the electromagnetic field are conserved separately (\href{\detokenize{https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11317519/}}{Nature Communications}). Hence

\[
\ell_{23}=n_1\ell_1+n_2\ell_2+n_3\ell_3 =-n_1+2n_2+n_3,
\]

and

\[
\sigma_{23} =n_1\sigma_1+n_2\sigma_2+n_3\sigma_3 =n_1-n_2+n_3.
\]

Because the emitted photon must have helicity $\sigma_{23}=\pm1$,

\[
n_1-n_2+n_3=\pm1.
\]

\subparagraph*{Left-helicity harmonic: $\sigma_{23}=+1$}

Solving

\[
n_1+n_2+n_3=23,\qquad n_1-n_2+n_3=1
\]

gives

\[
n_2=11,\qquad n_1+n_3=12.
\]

Writing $n_1=k$ and $n_3=12-k$,

\[
\ell_{23} =-k+2(11)+(12-k) =34-2k, \qquad k=0,1,\ldots,12.
\]

Therefore,

\[
{ \sigma_{23}=+1,\qquad \ell_{23}\in\{10,12,14,\ldots,34\}. }
\]

\subparagraph*{Right-helicity harmonic: $\sigma_{23}=-1$}

Similarly,

\[
n_2=12,\qquad n_1+n_3=11.
\]

With $n_1=k$ and $n_3=11-k$,

\[
\ell_{23} =-k+2(12)+(11-k) =35-2k, \qquad k=0,1,\ldots,11.
\]

Thus,

\[
{ \sigma_{23}=-1,\qquad \ell_{23}\in\{13,15,17,\ldots,35\}. }
\]

The strength and phase of each mode depend on the pulse intensities, relative carrier phases, radial profiles, gas species, microscopic dipole response, and macroscopic phase matching. Mixing vortex modes in gas HHG generally produces an OAM spectrum whose weights depend on precisely these quantities (\href{\detokenize{https://journals.aps.org/pra/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevA.105.023107}}{Physical Review A}).

Moreover, isolated single-color circular pulses do not efficiently drive ordinary recollision-based gas HHG, because circular polarization prevents electron return (\href{\detokenize{https://link.aps.org/accepted/10.1103/PhysRevLett.119.063201}}{Physical Review Letters}). The relevant emission here would arise primarily where the counter-rotating components overlap and produce a locally noncircular field.

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{
\mathcal H_{23}
=\{(\ell,+1):\ell=10,12,\ldots,34\}
\cup
\{(\ell,-1):\ell=13,15,\ldots,35\}
}
\]

\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

Define

\[
z=\frac{4\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^2}, \qquad H(n,z)={}_2F_1\left(\frac{1-n}{2},1-\frac n2;2;z\right),
\]

so that

\[
f(n,\alpha)=(1+\alpha)^{n-1}H(n,z).
\]

We first treat $0<\alpha<1$, for which $0<z<1$.

\subparagraph*{1. Euler integral representation}

Euler's integral representation of the Gaussian hypergeometric function is given in \href{\detokenize{https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.6.E1}}{DLMF Section 15.6.1}. Here it gives

\[
H(n,z) = \frac{1}{ \Gamma\left(1-\frac n2\right) \Gamma\left(1+\frac n2\right)} \int_0^1 t^{-n/2}(1-t)^{n/2}(1-zt)^{-(1-n)/2}\,dt.
\]

Let

\[
P(n)= \frac{1}{ \Gamma\left(1-\frac n2\right) \Gamma\left(1+\frac n2\right)}.
\]

Using $\psi(x)=\Gamma'(x)/\Gamma(x)$,

\[
\frac{P'(n)}{P(n)} = \frac12\psi\left(1-\frac n2\right) -\frac12\psi\left(1+\frac n2\right).
\]

Consequently,

\[
P(0)=1, \qquad P'(0)=0.
\]

For the integrand,

\[
\Phi(n,t)=t^{-n/2}(1-t)^{n/2}(1-zt)^{-(1-n)/2},
\]

and hence

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial n}\log\Phi(n,t) = -\frac12\log t +\frac12\log(1-t) +\frac12\log(1-zt).
\]

At $n=0$,

\[
\Phi(0,t)=\frac1{\sqrt{1-zt}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
H_n'(0,z) = \frac12\int_0^1 \frac{ \log\left(\dfrac{(1-t)(1-zt)}{t}\right) }{ \sqrt{1-zt} }\,dt. \tag{1}
\]

Differentiation under the integral is justified because, in a neighborhood of $n=0$, the integrand and its $n$-derivative are bounded by integrable functions proportional to

\[
t^{-\varepsilon}(1-t)^{-\varepsilon} \left(1+|\log t|+|\log(1-t)|\right),
\]

while $1-zt\geq 1-z>0$.

\subparagraph*{2. Evaluate $H(0,z)$}

At $n=0$,

\[
H(0,z) = \int_0^1\frac{dt}{\sqrt{1-zt}} = \frac{2(1-\sqrt{1-z})}{z}.
\]

Now

\[
1-z = 1-\frac{4\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^2} = \frac{(1-\alpha)^2}{(1+\alpha)^2}.
\]

Because $0\leq\alpha\leq1$,

\[
\sqrt{1-z}=\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}.
\]

Thus, for $\alpha>0$,

\[
H(0,z) = \frac{ 2\left(1-\dfrac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}\right) }{ \dfrac{4\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^2} } =1+\alpha. \tag{2}
\]

It follows that $f(0,\alpha)=1$.

\subparagraph*{3. Evaluate the logarithmic integral}

Introduce

\[
q=\sqrt{1-z}=\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}, \qquad z=1-q^2.
\]

In (1), set

\[
s=\sqrt{1-zt}, \qquad t=\frac{1-s^2}{z}, \qquad dt=-\frac{2s}{z}\,ds.
\]

The endpoints become

\[
t=0\Longrightarrow s=1, \qquad t=1\Longrightarrow s=q.
\]

Moreover,

\[
1-t=\frac{s^2-q^2}{z}, \qquad 1-zt=s^2.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{(1-t)(1-zt)}{t} = \frac{s^2(s^2-q^2)}{1-s^2}.
\]

Equation (1) becomes

\[
H_n'(0,z) = \frac1z \int_q^1 \log\left( \frac{s^2(s^2-q^2)}{1-s^2} \right)ds. \tag{3}
\]

Write the integral in (3) as

\[
A(q)= 2\int_q^1\log s\,ds +\int_q^1\log(s-q)\,ds +\int_q^1\log(s+q)\,ds -\int_q^1\log(1-s)\,ds -\int_q^1\log(1+s)\,ds.
\]

Using

\[
\int \log x\,dx=x\log x-x,
\]

the individual terms are

\[
2\int_q^1\log s\,ds = -2-2q\log q+2q,
\]

\[
\int_q^1\log(s-q)\,ds = (1-q)\log(1-q)-(1-q),
\]

\[
\int_q^1\log(s+q)\,ds = (1+q)\log(1+q)-(1+q)-2q\log(2q)+2q,
\]

\[
-\int_q^1\log(1-s)\,ds = -(1-q)\log(1-q)+(1-q),
\]

and

\[
-\int_q^1\log(1+s)\,ds = -2\log2+2+(1+q)\log(1+q)-(1+q).
\]

Adding and simplifying,

\[
A(q) = 2\left[ q-1 +(1+q)\log\left(\frac{1+q}{2}\right) -2q\log q \right]. \tag{4}
\]

Since

\[
q-1=-\frac{2\alpha}{1+\alpha}, \qquad 1+q=\frac{2}{1+\alpha}, \qquad \frac{1+q}{2}=\frac1{1+\alpha},
\]

equation (4) becomes

\[
A(q) = -\frac4{1+\alpha} \left[ \alpha+\log(1+\alpha) +(1-\alpha)\log\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}\right) \right]. \tag{5}
\]

Because $H_n'(0,z)=A(q)/z$ and

\[
z=\frac{4\alpha}{(1+\alpha)^2},
\]

we obtain

\[
\frac{H_n'(0,z)}{1+\alpha} = -\frac1\alpha \left[ \alpha+\log(1+\alpha) +(1-\alpha)\log\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}\right) \right]. \tag{6}
\]

\subparagraph*{4. Differentiate $f(n,\alpha)$}

The product rule gives

\[
g(\alpha) = \frac1{1+\alpha} \left[ \log(1+\alpha)H(0,z)+H_n'(0,z) \right].
\]

Using $H(0,z)=1+\alpha$ from (2),

\[
g(\alpha) = \log(1+\alpha)+\frac{H_n'(0,z)}{1+\alpha}.
\]

Substituting (6),

\[
g(\alpha) = \log(1+\alpha) -\frac1\alpha \left[ \alpha+\log(1+\alpha) +(1-\alpha)\log\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}\right) \right].
\]

Expanding the last logarithm,

\[
\log\left(\frac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}\right) = \log(1-\alpha)-\log(1+\alpha),
\]

all terms involving $\log(1+\alpha)$ cancel, leaving

\[
g(\alpha) = -1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\log(1-\alpha), \qquad 0<\alpha<1. \tag{7}
\]

\subparagraph*{5. Endpoint $\alpha=0$}

When $\alpha=0$, the hypergeometric argument is zero. Therefore,

\[
f(n,0) = 1^{n-1}\,{}_2F_1\left(\frac{1-n}{2},1-\frac n2;2;0\right) =1.
\]

Hence

\[
g(0)=0.
\]

This also agrees with the continuous limit because

\[
\log(1-\alpha)=-\alpha+O(\alpha^2),
\]

so

\[
-1-\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\log(1-\alpha) =O(\alpha)\longrightarrow0.
\]

\subparagraph*{6. Endpoint $\alpha=1$}

At $\alpha=1$, the hypergeometric argument is $z=1$. Gauss's summation theorem, stated in \href{\detokenize{https://dlmf.nist.gov/15.4.E20}}{DLMF Section 15.4.20}, gives

\[
f(n,1) = 2^{n-1} \frac{ \Gamma\left(\frac12+n\right) }{ \Gamma\left(\frac{3+n}{2}\right) \Gamma\left(1+\frac n2\right) }.
\]

Since $f(0,1)=1$, logarithmic differentiation yields

\[
g(1) = \log2+\psi\left(\frac12\right) -\frac12\psi\left(\frac32\right) -\frac12\psi(1).
\]

The special values are

\[
\psi(1)=-\gamma, \qquad \psi\left(\frac12\right)=-\gamma-2\log2,
\]

as listed in \href{\detokenize{https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.4.E12}}{DLMF Section 5.4}, and the recurrence

\[
\psi(z+1)=\psi(z)+\frac1z
\]

from \href{\detokenize{https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.5.E2}}{DLMF Section 5.5.2} gives

\[
\psi\left(\frac32\right) = \psi\left(\frac12\right)+2.
\]

Consequently,

\[
g(1)=-1.
\]

This agrees with (7) under the standard limiting convention

\[
\lim_{x\to0^+}x\log x=0.
\]

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{
g(\alpha)=
\begin{cases}
0, & \alpha=0,\\
-1, & \alpha=1,\\
-1-\dfrac{(1-\alpha)\log(1-\alpha)}{\alpha}, & 0<\alpha<1.
\end{cases}
}
\]

\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

The first-harmonic continuum model and parameters used here agree with those employed in the tMoTe$_2$ literature; the corresponding plane-wave Hamiltonian is also given explicitly in the literature. \href{\detokenize{https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10895274/}}{PNAS continuum-model formulation}, \href{\detokenize{https://www.nature.com/articles/s42005-025-02483-6}}{parameter cross-check}.

\subparagraph*{1. Moiré scales}

For $\theta=3.5^\circ$,

\[
a_M=\frac{3.52\ {\rm \text{\AA}}} {2\sin(1.75^\circ)} =57.6321442995\ {\rm \text{\AA}}.
\]

Consequently,

\[
b\equiv |\boldsymbol b_1| =\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}a_M} =0.125888036011\ {\rm \text{\AA}}^{-1}.
\]

The reciprocal vectors can be written as

\[
\boldsymbol b_1=b(1,0),\qquad \boldsymbol b_2=b\left(\frac12,\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right),
\]

and the Brillouin-zone area is

\[
A_{\rm BZ} = |\boldsymbol b_1\times\boldsymbol b_2| = \frac{\sqrt3}{2}b^2.
\]

The kinetic coefficient is

\[
\frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*} = \frac{1}{0.6}\frac{\hbar^2}{2m_e} = 12699.9403833\ {\rm meV\,\text{\AA}^2}.
\]

\subparagraph*{2. Plane-wave Hamiltonian}

Introduce the basis states $|l,\boldsymbol Q\rangle$, where

\[
\boldsymbol Q_t=\boldsymbol q_1+n\boldsymbol b_1+m\boldsymbol b_2,
\]

and

\[
\boldsymbol Q_b=-\boldsymbol q_1+n\boldsymbol b_1+m\boldsymbol b_2.
\]

Imposing

\[
|\boldsymbol Q_l|<4.1|\boldsymbol b_1|
\]

gives $63$ momenta in each layer and hence a $126\times126$ Hamiltonian at every $\boldsymbol k$.

With $s_b=-1$ and $s_t=+1$, the intralayer matrix elements are

\[
\adjustbox{max width=\linewidth}{$\displaystyle \begin{aligned}
H^{(l)}_{\boldsymbol Q,\boldsymbol Q'}(\boldsymbol k)
={}&
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}
|\boldsymbol k-\boldsymbol Q|^2
\delta_{\boldsymbol Q,\boldsymbol Q'}
\\
&+
V\sum_{i=1}^3
\left[
e^{is_l\psi}\,
\delta_{\boldsymbol Q',\,\boldsymbol Q+\boldsymbol g_i}
+
e^{-is_l\psi}\,
\delta_{\boldsymbol Q',\,\boldsymbol Q-\boldsymbol g_i}
\right].
\end{aligned}$}
\]

The interlayer block follows from the Fourier factor $e^{-i\boldsymbol q_i\cdot\boldsymbol r}$:

\[
H^{bt}_{\boldsymbol Q_b,\boldsymbol Q_t} = w\sum_{i=1}^3 \delta_{\boldsymbol Q_b-\boldsymbol Q_t,\boldsymbol q_i}, \qquad H^{tb}=(H^{bt})^\dagger.
\]

Diagonalizing this matrix at every momentum and sorting the energies from highest to lowest defines the top three bands.

\subparagraph*{3. Chern numbers}

For each isolated band, define the normalized lattice link

\[
U_\mu^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k) = \frac{ \langle u_{n,\boldsymbol k} | u_{n,\boldsymbol k+\Delta\boldsymbol k_\mu}\rangle }{ \left| \langle u_{n,\boldsymbol k} | u_{n,\boldsymbol k+\Delta\boldsymbol k_\mu}\rangle \right| },
\]

where

\[
\Delta\boldsymbol k_1=\frac{\boldsymbol b_1}{L}, \qquad \Delta\boldsymbol k_2=\frac{\boldsymbol b_2}{L}.
\]

The gauge-invariant plaquette flux is

\[
F_{12}^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k) = \operatorname{Arg} \left[ U_1^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k) U_2^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k+\Delta\boldsymbol k_1) U_1^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k+\Delta\boldsymbol k_2)^{-1} U_2^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k)^{-1} \right],
\]

and

\[
C_n=\frac{1}{2\pi}\sum_{\boldsymbol k}F_{12}^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k).
\]

At Brillouin-zone boundaries, the plane-wave coefficients are translated according to

\[
u_{l,\boldsymbol Q}(\boldsymbol k+\boldsymbol b_\alpha) = u_{l,\boldsymbol Q-\boldsymbol b_\alpha}(\boldsymbol k).
\]

The resulting Chern numbers, from the top band downward, are

\[
(C_1,C_2,C_3)=(1,1,-2).
\]

Their sum vanishes,

\[
C_1+C_2+C_3=0,
\]

as expected for this three-band group. Reversing the valley or the Berry-curvature orientation gives the globally reversed sequence $(-1,-1,2)$, consistent with reported tMoTe$_2$ conventions. \href{\detokenize{https://journals.aps.org/prx/pdf/10.1103/PhysRevX.13.031037}}{PRX topology convention}.

\subparagraph*{4. Integrated quantum metric of the top band}

Only the kinetic term depends explicitly on $\boldsymbol k$. With

\[
\kappa\equiv\frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*},
\]

its derivatives in the plane-wave basis are diagonal:

\[
D_i\equiv\frac{\partial H}{\partial k_i}
=-2\kappa(k_i-Q_i)\delta_{ll'}\delta_{\boldsymbol Q\boldsymbol Q'}.
\]

For an isolated band $n$, first-order perturbation theory gives the gauge-invariant metric

\[
g_{ij}^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k)
=\operatorname{Re}\sum_{m\ne n}
\frac{\langle u_n|D_i|u_m\rangle\langle u_m|D_j|u_n\rangle}
{(E_n-E_m)^2}.
\]

Thus the trace needed for the top band is evaluated directly from the full eigensystem at each mesh point:

\[
\operatorname{Tr}g^{(n)}(\boldsymbol k)
=\sum_{m\ne n}
\frac{|\langle u_m|D_x|u_n\rangle|^2+|\langle u_m|D_y|u_n\rangle|^2}
{(E_n-E_m)^2}.
\]

This avoids the finite-link bias of estimating derivatives from neighboring eigenvector overlaps. The requested $60\times60$ Brillouin-zone quadrature is

\[
\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal G
\simeq \frac{A_{\rm BZ}}{60^2}
\sum_{l_1,l_2}\operatorname{Tr}g(\boldsymbol k_{l_1l_2}).
\]

Numerically,

\[
\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal G=10.5177255472,
\]

which rounds to $10.52$. This quantity is dimensionless because $g_{ij}$ has units of length squared while $d^2k$ has units of inverse length squared.

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{
\begin{gathered}
(C_1,C_2,C_3)=(1,1,-2),\\
\operatorname{Tr}\mathcal{G}=10.52
\end{gathered}
}
\]

# Problem setup:

Consider a noisy distributed quantum sensing scenario as follows. The quantum sensor network contains $d$ sensor nodes, and each node contains $n$ sensor qubits. There is a potentially different parameter to be encoded on each sensor node locally. Our sensing objective is to estimate the scaled average of all $d$ local parameters, i.e., supposing that the parameters are $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_d$, we want to estimate $\theta_1 = (\sum_{i=1}^d x_i) / \sqrt{d}$. The quantum network will distribute a $d$-qubit Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state to the $d$ sensor nodes, while each sensor node will hold one qubit of the GHZ state. Then each sensor node further performs local entanglement generation between the qubit from the $d$-qubit GHZ state and the remaining $n-1$ sensor qubits. The final state is the initial probe state, which we assume to be an $nd$-qubit noisy GHZ state across the quantum sensor network. In other words, we assume that the dephasing rate is homogeneous across the entire sensor network, while the angular frequency is the same for each qubit on one node but can be generally different between nodes.

# Main problem:

Suppose that the noisy sensing dynamics has duration $t$, and each local parameter is the accumulated phase, i.e. $x_i = \omega^{(i)} t$. What is the quantum Fisher information for $\theta_1$? Do not explicitly include $\gamma$ and $t$ in the final expression. Instead, you may use another variable $q = (1 + e^{-\gamma t}) / 2$.

\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

The depolarized-GHZ fidelity convention and the model $F(n)=Fk^{n-1}$ match the formulation analyzed in the primary distributed-sensing study by Zang et al. \href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.17089}}{Quantum Advantage in Distributed Sensing with Noisy Quantum Networks}.

\subparagraph*{1. Initial depolarized GHZ state}

Let

\[
N=nd,\qquad D=2^N,\qquad f=F(n)=Fk^{n-1}.
\]

Define

\[
|\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}\rangle = \frac{|0\rangle^{\otimes N}+|1\rangle^{\otimes N}}{\sqrt2}.
\]

A depolarized GHZ state whose actual GHZ fidelity is $f$ is

\[
\rho_0 = f|\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}\rangle\langle\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}| + \beta\left( I_D- |\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}\rangle\langle\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}| \right),
\]

where

\[
\beta=\frac{1-f}{D-1}.
\]

Indeed,

\[
\langle\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}|\rho_0|\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}\rangle=f.
\]

This is equivalently a mixture with the maximally mixed state,

\[
\rho_0 = V|\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}\rangle\langle\mathrm{GHZ}_N^{+}| +(1-V)\frac{I_D}{D},
\]

with visibility

\[
V=\frac{Df-1}{D-1}=f-\beta.
\]

\subparagraph*{2. Single-qubit dephasing channel}

For a single-qubit off-diagonal matrix element, the Lindblad equation gives

\[
\frac{d}{dt}\rho_{01} = -\left(\gamma+i\omega^{(i)}\right)\rho_{01}.
\]

Hence

\[
\rho_{01}(t) = e^{-\gamma t}e^{-i\omega^{(i)}t}\rho_{01}(0).
\]

Equivalently, the dephasing part is the phase-flip channel

\[
\mathcal E_q(\rho)=q\rho+(1-q)\sigma_z\rho\sigma_z, \qquad q=\frac{1+e^{-\gamma t}}{2},
\]

because it transforms the single-qubit coherence as

\[
|0\rangle\langle1| \longmapsto \bigl[q-(1-q)\bigr]|0\rangle\langle1| = (2q-1)|0\rangle\langle1|.
\]

The global GHZ coherence differs on all $N=nd$ qubits. Independent dephasing therefore gives

\[
|0\rangle^{\otimes N}\langle1|^{\otimes N} \longmapsto (2q-1)^N |0\rangle^{\otimes N}\langle1|^{\otimes N}.
\]

Set

\[
s=(2q-1)^N=(2q-1)^{nd}.
\]

\subparagraph*{3. Phase encoded by the GHZ state}

The encoding unitary is

\[
U(\boldsymbol{x}) = \exp\left[ -\frac{i}{2} \sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i \sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_z^{(i,k)} \right].
\]

Since every node contains $n$ qubits,

\[
U(\boldsymbol{x})|0\rangle^{\otimes N} = e^{-\frac{in}{2}\sum_i x_i}|0\rangle^{\otimes N},
\]

while

\[
U(\boldsymbol{x})|1\rangle^{\otimes N} = e^{+\frac{in}{2}\sum_i x_i}|1\rangle^{\otimes N}.
\]

Thus the relative GHZ phase is

\[
\phi=n\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i.
\]

Using

\[
\theta_1=\frac{1}{\sqrt d}\sum_{i=1}^{d}x_i,
\]

we obtain

\[
\phi=n\sqrt d\,\theta_1, \qquad \frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta_1}=n\sqrt d.
\]

\subparagraph*{4. Parameter-dependent block of the density matrix}

Only the subspace spanned by

\[
|\bar0\rangle=|0\rangle^{\otimes N}, \qquad |\bar1\rangle=|1\rangle^{\otimes N}
\]

contains phase information. In this subspace, after encoding and dephasing,

\[
\rho_{\mathrm{GHZ}}(\theta_1)
=
\frac12
\begin{pmatrix}
f+\beta &
(f-\beta)s\,e^{-i\phi}\\[2mm]
(f-\beta)s\,e^{i\phi} &
f+\beta
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

All remaining $D-2$ eigenvalues equal $\beta$ and are independent of $\theta_1$, so they contribute zero QFI.

The two parameter-relevant eigenvalues are

\[
\lambda_\pm = \frac12\left[ f+\beta\pm(f-\beta)s \right].
\]

For the spectral QFI formula,

\[
\mathcal F_{\theta_1} = \sum_{a,b} \frac{2}{\lambda_a+\lambda_b} \left| \left\langle a\left| \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\theta_1} \right|b\right\rangle \right|^2,
\]

only the two off-diagonal terms between the $\lambda_+$ and $\lambda_-$ eigenvectors contribute. Their magnitude is

\[
\left| \left\langle +\left| \frac{\partial\rho}{\partial\theta_1} \right|-\right\rangle \right| = \frac{|f-\beta|s}{2} \left|\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta_1}\right|.
\]

Because

\[
\lambda_++\lambda_-=f+\beta,
\]

the QFI becomes

\[
\mathcal F_{\theta_1} = \frac{(f-\beta)^2s^2}{f+\beta} \left(\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial\theta_1}\right)^2.
\]

Substituting $s=(2q-1)^{nd}$ and $\partial_{\theta_1}\phi=n\sqrt d$,

\[
\mathcal F_{\theta_1} = dn^2(2q-1)^{2nd} \frac{(f-\beta)^2}{f+\beta}.
\]

Using $D=2^{nd}$ and $\beta=(1-f)/(D-1)$,

\[
f-\beta = \frac{Df-1}{D-1},
\]

\[
f+\beta = \frac{(D-2)f+1}{D-1}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{(f-\beta)^2}{f+\beta} = \frac{(Df-1)^2} {(D-1)\bigl[(D-2)f+1\bigr]}.
\]

Finally, substitute

\[
D=2^{nd}, \qquad f=Fk^{n-1}.
\]

As a consistency check, when $F=k=q=1$,

\[
\mathcal F_{\theta_1}=dn^2,

which is the ideal GHZ result for the scaled average.

\[
N(25000) = 75.1009281083.
\]

Thus the accumulated logarithmic scale-factor growth at the requested endpoint is $75.1009281083$ e-folds.

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{N(25000)=75.1009281083}
\]

# Problem setup:
Consider $Z_N$ ($N$ is any integer) parafermion zero-mode operators on four sites $\alpha_i$ with $i=1,2,3,4$ and a four-stage tunneling process described by

$
H_{34}\rightarrow H_{23} \rightarrow H_{12}\rightarrow H_{13}\rightarrow H_{34},
$

where
$
H_{ij}=t\left(e^{-i\phi_{ij}/N}\alpha_i^\dagger\alpha_j+H.c.\right)
$, $\phi_{ij}$ is a phase between sites $i$ and $j$, and $H.c.$ stands for Hermitian conjugate. This tunneling process is followed by a permutation between zero modes $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$ and $(\alpha_3,\alpha_4)$, respectively.

# Main problem:
Find the phase between the initial ground state of the process $|\psi^i(q)\rangle$ and final ground state of the process $|\psi^f(q)\rangle$, where $q$ is the fusion channel between the unpaired zero modes. Your answer should depend on $k_{ij}\in Z_N$, where $k_{ij}<-\frac{\phi_{ij}}{2\pi}<k_{ij}+1$. Note that, for a Josephson phase between sites i and j, k_ij is a ground-state fusion channel.
reference_solution:
\subsubsection*{Solution}
Let

\[
\omega=e^{2\pi i/N},
\]

and use the standard parafermion algebra

\[
\alpha_i^N=1, \qquad \alpha_i\alpha_j=\omega\,\alpha_j\alpha_i \quad (i<j).
\]

This convention agrees with the usual parity-operator formulation of $\mathbb Z_N$ parafermion braiding; see \href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/html/1511.02704v1}}{Hutter and Loss}, particularly their Eqs. (1), (6), and (23). Adiabatic exchange acts as a non-Abelian geometric phase in the degenerate ground-state manifold, as discussed for parafermion tunneling protocols in \href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09602}}{Hong et al.}.

\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

\subparagraph*{1. Fusion-parity operators}

For $i<j$, define

\[
Q_{ij} = \omega^{(N+1)/2}\alpha_i\alpha_j^\dagger, \qquad Q_{ij}^N=1.
\]

A fusion state with channel $p\in\mathbb Z_N$ satisfies

\[
Q_{ij}|p\rangle=\omega^p|p\rangle.
\]

Using $\alpha_j\alpha_i^\dagger=\omega\alpha_i^\dagger\alpha_j$,

\[
Q_{ij}^\dagger = \omega^{-(N+1)/2}\alpha_j\alpha_i^\dagger = \omega^{(1-N)/2}\alpha_i^\dagger\alpha_j,
\]

so

\[
\alpha_i^\dagger\alpha_j = \omega^{(N-1)/2}Q_{ij}^\dagger.
\]

Consequently, in the $Q_{ij}=\omega^p$ sector,

\[
E_p = 2t\cos\!\left[ \frac{\pi(N-1)-\phi_{ij}-2\pi p}{N} \right].
\]

Write

\[
-\frac{\phi_{ij}}{2\pi}=k_{ij}+\delta, \qquad 0<\delta<1.
\]

For $p=k_{ij}$,

\[
E_{k_{ij}} = 2t\cos\!\left[ \frac{\pi(N-1+2\delta)}{N} \right],
\]

which is the level closest to the minimum of the cosine. Hence the ground-state projector of $H_{ij}$ is

\[
P_{ij}^{(k_{ij})} = \frac1N\sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \omega^{-k_{ij}n}Q_{ij}^{\,n}.
\]

Thus $k_{ij}$ is precisely the ground-state fusion channel stated in the problem.

\subparagraph*{2. Convenient basis}

Choose basis states $|x,y\rangle$ satisfying

\[
Q_{12}|x,y\rangle=\omega^x|x,y\rangle, \qquad Q_{34}|x,y\rangle=\omega^y|x,y\rangle.
\]

The initial state is therefore

\[
|\psi^i(q)\rangle=|q,k_{34}\rangle.
\]

The relevant parity algebra is

\[
Q_{12}Q_{23}=\omega Q_{23}Q_{12},
\]

and one may choose the phases of $|x,y\rangle$ so that

\[
Q_{23}|x,y\rangle=|x+1,y-1\rangle.
\]

Moreover,

\[
Q_{13} = \omega^{(N-1)/2}Q_{12}Q_{23},
\]

and hence

\[
Q_{13}|x,y\rangle = \omega^{x+(N+1)/2}|x+1,y-1\rangle.
\]

Iterating this action gives

\[
Q_{13}^{m}|a,y\rangle = \omega^{ma+\frac{m(m+N)}2} |a+m,y-m\rangle.
\]

All channel labels and additions are understood modulo $N$.

\subparagraph*{3. Apply the tunneling sequence}

For compactness, set

\[
a=k_{12},\qquad b=k_{13},\qquad c=k_{23},\qquad d=k_{34}.
\]

The normalized ground-space transport operator is proportional to

\[
U = N^2P_{34}^{(d)} P_{13}^{(b)} P_{12}^{(a)} P_{23}^{(c)} P_{34}^{(d)}.
\]

The factor $N^2$ removes the magnitude $N^{-2}$ from the four mutually unbiased ground-space projections.

First,

\[
P_{23}^{(c)}|q,d\rangle = \frac1N \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \omega^{-cn}|q+n,d-n\rangle.
\]

Applying $P_{12}^{(a)}$ selects

\[
n=a-q.
\]

Therefore,

\[
P_{12}^{(a)}P_{23}^{(c)}|q,d\rangle = \frac1N \omega^{-c(a-q)} |a,d-a+q\rangle.
\]

Next, in $P_{13}^{(b)}$, the final $P_{34}^{(d)}$ selects the power

\[
m=q-a,
\]

because $Q_{13}^m$ changes

\[
|a,d-a+q\rangle \longrightarrow |a+m,d-a+q-m\rangle = |q,d\rangle.
\]

The resulting unnormalized amplitude is

\[
\frac{1}{N^2} \omega^{-c(a-q)} \omega^{-bm} \omega^{ma+\frac{m(m+N)}2}.
\]

Since $m=q-a$ and $-c(a-q)=cm$, its exponent is

\[
\begin{aligned}
E(q)
&=
m(c-b+a)+\frac{m(m+N)}2\\
&=
\frac{q-a}{2}
\left[q+a+N+2(c-b)\right].
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the normalized braid eigenvalue is

\[
e^{i\theta(q)} = \omega^{E(q)} = \exp\!\left[ \frac{i\pi}{N} (q-k_{12}) \left( q+k_{12}+N+2k_{23}-2k_{13} \right) \right].
\]

Equivalently, completing the square,

\[
e^{i\theta(q)} = \exp\!\left\{ \frac{i\pi}{N} \left[ \left(q+k_{23}-k_{13}+\frac N2\right)^2 - \left(k_{12}+k_{23}-k_{13}+\frac N2\right)^2 \right] \right\}.
\]

The result is independent of $k_{34}$: that channel fixes the initially paired modes, but cancels because $Q_{23}$ and $Q_{13}$ conserve the total fusion channel $x+y$. Similarly, $t$ only controls the excitation gap and not the universal braiding phase.

An unspecified interpolation time can add a common, $q$-independent dynamical phase. The expression above is the fusion-channel-dependent geometric phase, normalized so that $\theta(k_{12})=0$. Reversing the braid orientation complex-conjugates it.

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{
e^{i\theta(q)}=
\exp\!\left[
\frac{i\pi}{N}(q-k_{12})
\left(q+k_{12}+N+2k_{23}-2k_{13}\right)
\right]
}
\]

Consider a (1+1)-D CFT on a torus that consists of right- and left-moving edges of a Moore-Read state at filling fraction $\nu=1/k$. The primary fields are labeled by $(j_L,n_L,j_R,n_R)$, where $j_{L/R}=0,1/2,1$, $n_{L/R}\in Z_{2k}$  and the electron operators in the theory are $(1,2k,0,0)$ and $(0,0,1,2k)$.

# Main problem:
Given $k=2$, find the expectation values of Verlinde lines assuming the identity operator has expectation value 1. Return your answer as a tuple $(j_L,n_L,j_R,n_R,\lambda_{(j_L,n_L,j_R,n_R)})$, where $\lambda_{(j_L,n_L,j_R,n_R)}$ is the expectation value.

# Problem setup:
Consider the following spin model on a torus
\begin{equation}
Z^{(n)}_{\text{RM},\ \alpha}\left[J\right]=\sum_{\left\{\eta_{ij}=\pm 1\right\}}P[\eta]\sum_{\left\{ \sigma^{(f)}=\pm1\right\}|_{f=1, \dots n-1} }e^{J\sum_{f=1}^{n-1}\sum_{\langle i,\ j\rangle}\eta_{ij}\sigma^{(f)}_{i}\sigma^{(f)}_{j}},\ \text{with}\ P[\eta]=\prod_{\langle i, j \rangle}\frac{e^{J\eta_{ij}}}{2\cosh J},
\end{equation}
where $\sigma^{(f)}_{i}=\pm1$ are the $f$-flavor Ising spins on a square lattice with
$N$ sites, f=1,2,…n, n denotes the number of flavor, $\eta_{ij}$ is a bond variable associated with $ij$, and $J \geq 0$ is a coupling constant. Here, $\alpha=\text{PP},\ \text{AP},\ \text{PA},\ \text{AA}$
indicates, for each flavor, an independent choice of boundary conditions (periodic $\text{P}$ or anti-periodic
$\text{A}$ along the non-contractable loop). For brevity, we drop the subscript $\alpha$ when all flavors take periodic-periodic boundary conditions. $Z^{(n)}_{\text{RM}}$ is defined as partition function when all flavors take the periodic-periodic boundary conditions. $y$ is the free energy from twisting boundary conditions, defined as
\begin{equation}
y= -\frac{2}{n-1}\log_2(\frac{\sum_\alpha Z^{(n)}_{\text{RM}, \alpha}}{2^{n-1}Z^{(n)}_{\text{RM}}}).
\end{equation}

# Main problem:

Calculate the value $J$ for $n=3$ where $y=0$ in a $100\times 100$-site lattice to three decimal places.
reference_solution:
\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

For $n=3$, there are $n-1=2$ explicit Ising flavors. This case is exactly equivalent to the ferromagnetic four-state Potts model. This equivalence is consistent with the established mapping of the two-replica model on the Nishimori line to the $2^2$-state Potts model (\href{\detokenize{https://www.lptmc.jussieu.fr/files/maillard/Nishimori_a33801.pdf}}{Maillard-Nemoto-Nishimori}).

\subparagraph*{1. Perform the bond-variable sum}

For a given bond $\langle i,j\rangle$, define

\[
u_f=\sigma_i^{(f)}\sigma_j^{(f)}\in\{-1,+1\}, \qquad f=1,2.
\]

Combining the disorder distribution with the two-flavor Boltzmann factor gives the local weight

\[
\begin{aligned}
w(u_1,u_2)
&=\sum_{\eta=\pm1}
\frac{e^{J\eta}}{2\cosh J}
e^{J\eta(u_1+u_2)}\\
&=\frac{1}{2\cosh J}
\sum_{\eta=\pm1}e^{J\eta(1+u_1+u_2)}\\
&=\frac{\cosh\!\left[J(1+u_1+u_2)\right]}{\cosh J}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The four possibilities are

\[
w(u_1,u_2)=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\cosh(3J)}{\cosh J},&u_1=u_2=+1,\\[6pt]
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

\subparagraph*{2. Identify the four-state Potts model}

Introduce a four-state composite spin

\[
S_i=\left(\sigma_i^{(1)},\sigma_i^{(2)}\right).
\]

The condition $u_1=u_2=+1$ is precisely $S_i=S_j$. Therefore

\[
w(S_i,S_j)=e^{K\delta_{S_i,S_j}},
\]

where the Potts coupling $K$ satisfies

\[
e^K=\frac{\cosh(3J)}{\cosh J}.
\]

Thus,

\[
Z_{\mathrm{RM}}^{(3)} = \sum_{\{S_i=1,\ldots,4\}} \exp\left(K\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}\delta_{S_i,S_j}\right).
\]

\subparagraph*{3. Apply torus duality and the condition $y=0$}

Let

\[
v=e^K-1.
\]

For the square-lattice $q$-state Potts model, duality gives

\[
vv^*=q.
\]

On a finite torus, duality mixes all twisted boundary-condition sectors. At the self-dual coupling, the untwisted partition function obeys

\[
\sum_{\alpha} Z_\alpha=qZ_{\mathrm{PP}},
\]

where the sum includes the independent twists of both Ising flavors around both torus cycles. Toroidal twisted sectors are known to transform into one another under Potts duality (\href{\detokenize{https://weizmann.esploro.exlibrisgroup.com/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/DUALITY-TWISTED-BOUNDARY-CONDITIONS-IN-N-STATE-POTTS/993262644703596}}{Schütz, Journal of Physics A 26, 4555}); see also the standard Potts duality review by \href{\detokenize{https://journals.aps.org/rmp/abstract/10.1103/RevModPhys.54.235}}{F. Y. Wu}.

Here $q=2^{n-1}=4$, so at the self-dual point,

\[
\sum_\alpha Z_{\mathrm{RM},\alpha}^{(3)} = 4Z_{\mathrm{RM}}^{(3)}.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\begin{aligned}
y
&=-\frac{2}{3-1}
\log_2\left(
\frac{\sum_\alpha Z_{\mathrm{RM},\alpha}^{(3)}}
{2^{3-1}Z_{\mathrm{RM}}^{(3)}}
\right)\\
&=-\log_2\left(\frac{4Z_{\mathrm{RM}}^{(3)}}{4Z_{\mathrm{RM}}^{(3)}}\right)
=0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Because this torus duality relation is a finite-lattice identity, the $100\times100$ size introduces no shift in the zero.

\subparagraph*{4. Solve the self-dual equation}

For $q=4$,

\[
v_c=\sqrt{q}=2,
\]

and hence

\[
e^{K_c}=1+v_c=3.
\]

Using the mapping to the original coupling,

\[
\frac{\cosh(3J_c)}{\cosh J_c}=3.
\]

With

\[
\cosh(3J)=4\cosh^3J-3\cosh J,
\]

we obtain

\[
4\cosh^2J_c-3=3,
\]

so

\[
\cosh^2J_c=\frac32.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\cosh(2J_c)=2\cosh^2J_c-1=2.
\]

Since $J\geq0$,

\[
J_c=\frac12\operatorname{arcosh}(2) =\frac12\ln(2+\sqrt3).
\]

Numerically,

\[
J_c=0.658478948462408\ldots
\]

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{J=0.658}
\]

\subsubsection*{Solution}
\paragraph*{Step-by-Step Derivation}

\subparagraph*{1. Interpretation of the interaction}

A genuine on-site Hubbard interaction is local in real space:

\[
H_U=U\sum_{\mathbf R,a=1,2} n_{\mathbf R a\uparrow}n_{\mathbf R a\downarrow}.
\]

Its momentum-space form is

\[
H_U= \frac{U}{N_c} \sum_{a,\mathbf k,\mathbf k',\mathbf q} c^\dagger_{a,\mathbf k+\mathbf q,\uparrow} c^\dagger_{a,\mathbf k'-\mathbf q,\downarrow} c_{a,\mathbf k',\downarrow} c_{a,\mathbf k,\uparrow},
\]

where $N_c$ is the number of unit cells.

Thus the interaction written in the question,

\[
U\sum_{\mathbf k,a}n_{a\mathbf k\uparrow}n_{a\mathbf k\downarrow},
\]

is not the Fourier transform of an on-site Hubbard interaction: it omits momentum-transfer processes. The calculation below therefore uses the standard real-space Hubbard interpretation. This is also the interaction used in studies of this quarter-filled chiral $\pi$-flux Chern-Hubbard model \href{\detokenize{https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevB.99.014407}}{Su et al., Phys. Rev. B 99, 014407}.

\subparagraph*{2. Noninteracting Bloch Hamiltonian}

For either spin, write

\[
h(\mathbf k)=
\begin{pmatrix}
d_3(\mathbf k)&f(\mathbf k)\\
f^*(\mathbf k)&-d_3(\mathbf k)
\end{pmatrix},
\]

with

\[
d_3(\mathbf k)=2(\cos k_x-\cos k_y)
\]

and

\[
f(\mathbf k)=\sqrt2\left[ e^{i\pi/4}\left(1+e^{i(k_y-k_x)}\right) +e^{-i\pi/4}\left(e^{-ik_x}+e^{ik_y}\right) \right].
\]

This is the checkerboard/chiral-$\pi$-flux Chern-band Hamiltonian at the nearly optimal flat-band ratio $t_1/t_2=\sqrt2$, originally introduced in the checkerboard Chern-band construction \href{\detokenize{https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.106.236804}}{Neupert et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 106, 236804}.

Introduce

\[
u=\frac{k_x+k_y}{2},\qquad v=\frac{k_x-k_y}{2}.
\]

Then

\[
1+e^{i(k_y-k_x)} =1+e^{-2iv}=2e^{-iv}\cos v,
\]

and

\[
e^{-ik_x}+e^{ik_y} =e^{-iv}\left(e^{-iu}+e^{iu}\right) =2e^{-iv}\cos u.
\]

Therefore

\[
f(\mathbf k) = 2\sqrt2\,e^{-iv} \left(e^{i\pi/4}\cos v+e^{-i\pi/4}\cos u\right).
\]

Since the relative phase is $\pi/2$,

\[
|f(\mathbf k)|^2 =8\left(\cos^2u+\cos^2v\right).
\]

Moreover,

\[
d_3 =2[\cos(u+v)-\cos(u-v)] =-4\sin u\sin v.
\]

The two bands are consequently

\[
\varepsilon_\pm(\mathbf k) =\pm D(\mathbf k)-\mu,
\]

where

\[
D^2(\mathbf k) = 8(\cos^2u+\cos^2v) +16\sin^2u\sin^2v.
\]

Setting $x=\cos^2u$ and $y=\cos^2v$,

\[
D^2=16-8x-8y+16xy.
\]

Because this is bilinear on $0\leq x,y\leq1$, its extrema occur at the corners:

\[
8\leq D^2\leq16.
\]

Hence

\[
2\sqrt2\leq D\leq4.
\]

The lower-band width is therefore exactly

\[
W=\max\varepsilon_- -\min\varepsilon_- =4-2\sqrt2 =1.17157287525381.
\]

The separation between the two bands is

\[
\Delta=2D_{\min}=4\sqrt2 =5.65685424949238.
\]

At quarter filling there is one electron per two-site unit cell, so the spin-degenerate lower band is half-filled. A fully polarized state fills exactly one spin copy of the lower Chern band.

\subparagraph*{3. Criterion for ferromagnetism}

Let $u_a(\mathbf k)$ be the lower-band Bloch eigenvector and $d^\dagger_{\mathbf k\sigma}$ its creation operator. The fully polarized state is

\[
|\mathrm{FM}\rangle = \prod_{\mathbf k} d^\dagger_{\mathbf k\uparrow}|0\rangle.
\]

It has zero Hubbard energy because no site contains both spins.

To test its stability, use the one-spin-flip basis

\[
|\mathbf k;\mathbf q\rangle = d^\dagger_{\mathbf k-\mathbf q,\downarrow} d_{\mathbf k,\uparrow}|\mathrm{FM}\rangle.
\]

After projecting the Hubbard interaction onto the lower band, the excitation matrix can be written as

\[
M(\mathbf q) = \operatorname{diag}_{\mathbf k} \left[ \varepsilon_-(\mathbf k-\mathbf q) -\varepsilon_-(\mathbf k) +\frac{U}{2} \right] -\frac{U}{N_c}\sum_{a=1}^{2} \mathbf v_a(\mathbf q)\mathbf v_a^\dagger(\mathbf q),
\]

where

\[
v_{a,\mathbf k}(\mathbf q) = u_a^*(\mathbf k)u_a(\mathbf k-\mathbf q).
\]

The ferromagnetic state is stable provided

\[
\lambda_{\min}[M(\mathbf q)]\geq0 \qquad\text{for every }\mathbf q.
\]

Consequently,

\[
\min_{\mathbf q\neq0} \lambda_{\min}[M(\mathbf q;U_c)]=0.
\]

This is the projected-band exact-diagonalization stability criterion used in the published analysis. The instability is caused by a spin-wave mode becoming soft \href{\detokenize{https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.11986}}{Su et al.}.

\subparagraph*{4. Numerical evaluation}

I evaluated the above matrix in the thermodynamic limit. The largest required interaction occurs for a long-wavelength diagonal mode,

\[
\mathbf q\rightarrow(0,0),\qquad q_x=q_y.
\]

Representative results, using the hopping units appearing in the question, are

\setlength{\tabcolsep}{3pt}
\begin{longtable}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.450\linewidth} >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{0.450\linewidth}@{}}
\toprule
$q_x=q_y$ & Critical $U(q)$ \\
\midrule
\endfirsthead
\toprule
$q_x=q_y$ & Critical $U(q)$ \\
\midrule
\endhead
$0.040$ & $2.81767352670527$ \\
$0.030$ & $2.81768266479253$ \\
$0.020$ & $2.81768916868757$ \\
$0.015$ & $2.81769144051183$ \\
$0.010$ & $2.81769306160911$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{longtable}
\endgroup

An extrapolation of the form

\[
U(q)=U_c+Aq^2+Bq^4+\cdots
\]

gives

\[
U_c=2.8176943579.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\frac{U_c}{W} = \frac{2.8176943579}{4-2\sqrt2} = 2.40505257284.
\]

The simpler Stoner/band-splitting estimate would give

\[
U_c^{\mathrm{rough}}\simeq2W =8-4\sqrt2 =2.34314575050762,
\]

but it neglects the collective spin-wave contribution and underestimates the projected-band result.

The projection is reasonably controlled here because

\[
U_c<\Delta, \qquad \frac{U_c}{\Delta}\simeq0.498,
\]

although the quoted value should not be regarded as an exact theorem for the unprojected many-body Hubbard model.

If the momentum-diagonal interaction in the question is intended literally, rather than as shorthand for the real-space Hubbard term, this $U_c$ does not apply and no unique conventional Hubbard critical interaction is specified.

\subsubsection*{Final Answer}

\[
\boxed{U_c=2.81769435790}
\]
